data.ruling: The refutation does not stand. The figure is tested by the P4 rule in tools/research/round1.js:314. Under that rule the list must name every requirement that IOBoard.md, the answers and the values found for research set for the function, and no listed value may be weaker than its source. V80's found value is a fact about the display, not a requirement on the link-supply switch. The answer is "No": the display's native USB-C VBUS is tied directly to its 5V net. Research.md's R5 row (line 314) says what follows from that answer: "If the display does not isolate its VBUS, R5 states it as a conflict". P2 did this in its report "display VBUS conflict". The direct connection puts a requirement on the switch in one direction only: the display back-feeding the IO board. The list names that requirement twice. "Reverse current blocked" comes from V266, which the owner answered "Yes" unconditionally, so it is stronger than anything conditioned on V80. "5 V back-fed with the input at 0 V" is up to 5.5 V on OUT, survived and blocked, from V81 and V266. The other direction, link power reaching the host's VBUS through Type_C2, is a property of the display that the switch cannot prevent. No answer and no IOBoard.md line sets a switch requirement for it. IOBoard.md:423 states it as "not specified as safe". The rule asks for requirements to be named, not for every value-found row to be cited. A value found for research that sets no part requirement leaves no gap in the list. The verifier itself states "No value in the list is weaker". V79's 4.5 V is carried as the switch's 90 mV share of the display-end budget: 4.825 V − 4.5 V = 325 mV, of which the switch takes 45 mOhm max × 2 A = 90 mV and the cable the remaining 235 mV. That is a derivation from V79, not a weakening of it. IOBoard.md:64 and 368–370 set 5 V, 2 A peak and 1.5 A continuous from the selected source, and the list names all three.
data.evidence: Research.md:314 (R5 row): "The display's supply blocks reverse current ... Whether the link supply then reaches the display's USB-C VBUS depends on the display's own power path ... If the display does not isolate its VBUS, R5 states it as a conflict." Research.md:786 V80, "R5, display supply", answer "for research". Research.md:972 V266: "Yes: the 5 V link supply blocks reverse current ... so the display's USB-C feeds nothing into the IO board". IOBoard.md:64: "Display supply | through the link cable, from the selected source ... 5 V (F6); 2 A peak, 1.5 A continuous". IOBoard.md:368: part TPS259474ARPWR. IOBoard.md:423: "Until it is known, connecting both at once is not specified as safe" (a statement on the pages, not a switch requirement). FU-2B1 P2-R5 return: V80 found "No. The native USB-C socket Type_C2 ties its VBUS pins to the display's 5V net with only a TVS to ground ... R5 states it as a conflict (report 'display VBUS conflict')". The display-supply requirement list holds "reverse current blocked" (V266) and "5 V back-fed with the input at 0 V: 5.5 V on OUT with IN at 0 V survived and blocked" (V81, V266). The display schematic was re-fetched with HTTP 200 and 2,027,038 bytes. Its text holds Type_C1, Type_C2, AO3401 (Q5, Q10), LTVS16H5.0ET5G and TJA1051T/3. The net tie itself was not re-traced, because text extraction does not carry the wiring. The ruling does not depend on it: the verifier's reading of V80 is accepted as stated. Rule text: tools/research/round1.js:314, "whether the function's requirement list names every requirement set for it by IOBoard.md, the answers and each value found for research whose row under 'Raised by P1' names the function, with no value weaker than theirs".
